profile.feeling: The everyday “have”: literally “at me, at you” — possession as location.

senses.def: to have — عِنْدَ + pronoun suffix: عِنْدِي “at me” = I have
at (someone’s place), near, with: عِنْدَ الطَّبِيبِ (at the doctor’s), عِنْدَ الْبَابِ (at the door)
at (a moment, a time of day): عِنْدَ الظُّهْرِ (at noon), عِنْدَ السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ (at five)

examples.tr: She has a brother and two sisters.

synonyms.nuance: at, with; لَدَيَّ = I have — the written, formal counterpart of عِنْدِي
for, belonging to: لِي أَخٌ = I have a brother — for relatives, rights and lasting relations
with: مَعِي قَلَمٌ = I have a pen (on me, right now)

etymology.text: A contraction of ع ن ن or ع ي ن (in the sense of viewing) and يَدَا (“hand”), i.e. “at hand, before one’s eyes”; compare لَدَى and لَدُنْ.

funFacts: عِنْدَمَا (“when”) is simply عِنْدَ + مَا.
Russian у меня есть and Turkish bende var say it the same way: “at me (there is)” — Greek, German and English use a verb.
Hebrew says יֵשׁ לִי (yesh li, “there is to me”), with the preposition “to” — the twin of Arabic لِي أَخٌ.
pitfalls: عِنْدَ is a preposition, not a verb: it does not change for tense. “I had” = كَانَ عِنْدِي; “I don’t have” = لَيْسَ عِنْدِي.
The thing you have is the grammatical subject, so it is nominative and usually indefinite: عِنْدِي جَزَرَةٌ (not جَزَرَةً).
Unvocalized عند can also be the verb عَنَدَ, “to be stubborn” (root of عِنَاد, stubbornness — Turkish inat).
subtleties: عِنْدِي is for what you own or keep at your place, لِي for relations and rights, مَعِي for what you carry right now.
“At” a place is فِي (فِي الْبَيْتِ, at home); “at” a person or a landmark is عِنْدَ (عِنْدَ صَدِيقِي, at my friend’s; عِنْدَ الْبَابِ, at the door).
For a moment in time عِنْدَ is as common as فِي: عِنْدَ الظُّهْرِ, عِنْدَ الْفَجْرِ (at dawn).

profile.feeling: The household family — parents and children; the word of forms, schools and the news.

senses.def: a dynasty, a ruling house (الْأُسْرَةُ الْحَاكِمَةُ)

examples.tr: The family lives in a flat.
He is from the ruling family.

synonyms.nuance: family — warmer, often the wider family with relatives; the common word in speech
one's people, kin: أَهْلِي (my family, my folks)

etymology.text: Wiktionary files it under the root ء س ر, the root of أَسَرَ (to take captive) and أَسِير (captive); it gives no further origin.

funFacts: Turkish esir (prisoner of war) is Arabic أَسِير, from the same root.
pitfalls: Unvocalized أسرة is also أَسِرَّة (beds, the plural of سَرِير) — the vowels and the šadda decide.
With a possessive the ة becomes ت: أُسْرَتِي, أُسْرَتُكَ.
subtleties: أُسْرَة is the family as a unit (sociology, forms: الْأُسْرَةُ النَّوَوِيَّةُ, the nuclear family); عَائِلَة is often the wider family.

profile.feeling: Family warmth, the big family, the family name.

senses.def: family (in general, often with the wider family)

examples.tr: We visit the family at the Eid.

synonyms.nuance: the household family as a unit — forms, statistics, the news
one's people, family: أَهْلِي

etymology.text: Wiktionary puts it under the root ع و ل, the root of عَالَ (to provide for, to support a family) and عِيَال (dependants, children); no older origin is given.

funFacts: Turkish aile (family) is this Arabic word.
pitfalls: The hamza sits on a yāʾ seat: عَائِلَة (ʿāʾila); the spelling عايلة is colloquial.
Possessive: عَائِلَتِي (ة → ت).
subtleties: In many dialects عَائِلَة (or عِيلَة) is the everyday word, and أُسْرَة sounds formal.

profile.feeling: Respectful and warm: “the two who gave birth” — father and mother together.

examples.tr: Being good to one's parents is a duty.

synonyms.nuance: the dual of أَب, also “parents” (father and mother)
family, folks — in many dialects “my parents” is أَهْلِي

etymology.text: The dual of وَالِد (father; parent), which Wiktionary derives from the active participle of وَلَدَ (to give birth) — root و ل د.

funFacts: Turkish ebeveyn (parents) is the other Arabic word, أَبَوَيْن; Turkish valide (mother, as in Valide Sultan) is وَالِدَة.
The masculine dual covers a man and a woman — Arabic lets the masculine stand for both.
pitfalls: It is a dual: وَالِدَانِ (nom.), وَالِدَيْنِ (acc., gen.). With a possessive the -ni drops: وَالِدَايَ (my parents), وَالِدَاكَ (your parents).
What agrees with it is dual too: وَالِدَايَ مُعَلِّمَانِ (two teachers).
subtleties: وَالِد / وَالِدَة alone are the respectful “father / mother”: وَالِدِي، وَالِدَتِي.

profile.feeling: The mother: tenderness, sacrifice — and the origin of things.

senses.def: origin, source; the main one (أُمُّ الْقُرَى, “mother of towns” = Mecca)
mother of (a woman called after her child: أُمُّ أَحْمَدَ)

examples.tr: Umm Kulthum is a famous singer.

phrases.text: الْأُمُّ مَدْرَسَةٌ إِذَا أَعْدَدْتَهَا أَعْدَدْتَ شَعْبًا طَيِّبَ الْأَعْرَاقِ
phrases.tr: A mother is a school: if you prepare her, you prepare a people of good stock.
Paradise lies under the feet of mothers.
phrases.meaning: honour your mother above all (a popular saying attributed to the Prophet)

synonyms.nuance: mother — respectful: وَالِدَتِي
mum — children's and family speech

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔimm-, from Proto-Afroasiatic *ʔim-; cognate with Hebrew אֵם (em) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: أُمَّة (nation, community — Turkish ümmet) is from the same root ء م م.
Hebrew אֵם (em) is the same word.
pitfalls: The šadda matters: أُمّ (umm, mother) — أَمْ (am) is “or” in questions.
Plural أُمَّهَات, with an extra -h-.
subtleties: A woman is often called after her eldest son, أُمُّ أَحْمَدَ — a warm, respectful way to address her.

profile.feeling: The father — protection, authority; and “father of” in names.

senses.def: father of (a man called after his child: أَبُو أَحْمَدَ)

examples.tr: Abu Ahmad is my father's friend.

collocations.tr: fathers and sons, parents and children

phrases.tr: whoever resembles his father has done no wrong

synonyms.nuance: father — respectful: وَالِدِي
dad — children's and family speech

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔabw-; cognate with Hebrew אָב (av) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English abbot comes from Aramaic אַבָּא (abba, father) through Greek and Latin — the same Semitic word.
Turkish ebeveyn (parents) is Arabic أَبَوَيْن, “the two fathers” = father and mother.
pitfalls: One of the “five nouns”: with a possessive it lengthens — أَبُوكَ (nom.), أَبَاكَ (acc.), أَبِيكَ (gen.); but “my father” is أَبِي in every case.
آبَاء means “fathers, forefathers”; “parents” is وَالِدَانِ or أَبَوَانِ.
subtleties: أَبُو in names and places: أَبُو بَكْرٍ, أَبُو ظَبْيٍ (Abu Dhabi).

profile.feeling: Son — lineage and pride; in names, “son of”.

senses.def: son of (in names: مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللّٰهِ)
a child of (a place or a group): اِبْنُ الْبَلَدِ, a local

examples.tr: The eldest son is an engineer.

collocations.tr: a cousin (son of a paternal uncle)
a local, a son of the country

phrases.meaning: a traveller, a wayfarer in need

synonyms.nuance: child; son — the everyday word
son — in official and news style: نَجْلُ الرَّئِيسِ

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *bin- (Wiktionary); cognate with Hebrew בֵּן (ben).

funFacts: Hebrew בֵּן (ben), as in Benjamin, is the same word.
Avicenna is Ibn Sīnā (اِبْنُ سِينَا): Latin kept only the name.
pitfalls: The first alif is a hamzat al-waṣl: after a vowel it is silent (عِنْدَهُمُ ابْنٌ), and between two names the word is written بْن: مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ سَلْمَانَ.
Plural أَبْنَاء (sons, children).
subtleties: Family words joined make new relatives: اِبْنُ عَمٍّ (cousin), اِبْنُ أَخٍ (nephew).

examples.tr: The youngest daughter is at school.
My cousin (my uncle's daughter) is a teacher.

synonyms.nuance: girl; daughter — the everyday word
daughter — very polite (invitations, formal speech): كَرِيمَتُهُ

etymology.text: The feminine of اِبْن (son), with the ending -a (ة); Wiktionary gives بَنَات as its plural and بِنْت as the other feminine.

funFacts: Arabic has two words for “daughter”, اِبْنَة and بِنْت; Hebrew has only בַּת (bat), the cognate of بِنْت.
pitfalls: Plural بَنَات, the plural of بِنْت too — there is no *اِبْنَات.
Hamzat al-waṣl, as in اِبْن: الِابْنَةُ, and the i- is silent after a vowel.
subtleties: اِبْنَة sounds formal and written; بِنْتِي is what parents say.

profile.feeling: Brother — blood, solidarity, and the friendly “brother!”.

examples.tr: Do you have brothers and sisters?

phrases.text: رُبَّ أَخٍ لَكَ لَمْ تَلِدْهُ أُمُّكَ
phrases.tr: many a brother of yours was not born of your mother
phrases.meaning: a true friend can be a brother

synonyms.nuance: full brother (same father and mother); also “brotherly” for countries

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔaḫw- (Wiktionary); cognate with Hebrew אָח (akh).

funFacts: Hebrew אָח (akh) is the same word.
The plural إِخْوَان (brethren) is the “Brotherhood” in الْإِخْوَانُ الْمُسْلِمُونَ.
pitfalls: One of the five nouns: أَخُوكَ (nom.), أَخَاكَ (acc.), أَخِيكَ (gen.) — but “my brother” is always أَخِي.
Plural إِخْوَة (brothers; siblings); إِخْوَان is “brethren, brothers in faith”.
subtleties: إِخْوَة for a mixed group means brothers and sisters: عِنْدِي ثَلَاثَةُ إِخْوَةٍ can include a sister.

pitfalls: Do not mix up عَمَّة (father's sister) and خَالَة (mother's sister).
Unvocalized عمة is also عِمَّة (turban).
subtleties: Plural عَمَّات; possessive عَمَّتِي.

profile.feeling: The mother's sister — “like a mother”; also a kind “auntie” for older women.

senses.def: “auntie”: a polite address to an older woman

examples.tr: My aunt (my mother's sister) is a teacher.
Thank you, auntie! (to an older woman)

phrases.tr: the maternal aunt is in the place of the mother
phrases.meaning: a mother's sister counts as a mother (a hadith)

profile.synonymsNone: MSA has no other word; colloquial forms such as خَالْتُو are the same word.

etymology.text: The feminine of خَال (maternal uncle) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Chinese 姨 (yí, 姨妈) is also the mother's sister — and 阿姨, like خَالَة, is said to older women in general.
pitfalls: False friend for Turkish speakers: Turkish hala (the father's sister) comes from خَالَة, but in Arabic خَالَة is the mother's sister (Turkish teyze).
Not the father's sister — that is عَمَّة.
subtleties: Plural خَالَات; possessive خَالَتِي.

profile.feeling: Kinship — the people close to you by blood or marriage.

senses.def: near, close (the same word as an adjective, lesson 12)

examples.tr: The house is close to here.

synonyms.nuance: a relative by marriage, an in-law
kin, family (collective)

etymology.text: A فَعِيل-type adjective from قَرُبَ (to be near); cognate with Hebrew קָרוֹב (karóv, “close, near”) and Amharic ቅርብ (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew קָרוֹב (karóv) also means both “near” and “relative” — the same Semitic word.
Turkish akraba (relatives) is the Arabic plural أَقْرِبَاء.
pitfalls: Two plurals: أَقْرِبَاء and the very common أَقَارِب (الْأَقَارِبُ) — both are diptotes: no -un, and -a for the indefinite genitive.
As a noun “relative”, as an adjective “near” (قَرِيبٌ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ) — the sentence decides.
subtleties: A female relative is قَرِيبَة; قَرَابَة is kinship.

absent.reason: Arabic has no word for “cousin”: it always says which parent's sibling the cousin comes from, with “son / daughter of” + the uncle or aunt.
absent.use: اِبْنُ عَمٍّ / بِنْتُ عَمٍّ (father's brother), اِبْنُ عَمَّةٍ / بِنْتُ عَمَّةٍ (father's sister), اِبْنُ خَالٍ / بِنْتُ خَالٍ (mother's brother), اِبْنُ خَالَةٍ / بِنْتُ خَالَةٍ (mother's sister) — “my cousin”: اِبْنُ عَمِّي, بِنْتُ خَالَتِي (the possessive goes on the last word).

absent.reason: No single word: a nephew is “the brother's son” or “the sister's son”.
absent.use: اِبْنُ الْأَخِ (brother's son), اِبْنُ الْأُخْتِ (sister's son); “my nephew”: اِبْنُ أَخِي / اِبْنُ أُخْتِي.

absent.reason: No single word: a niece is “the brother's daughter” or “the sister's daughter”.
absent.use: بِنْتُ الْأَخِ (brother's daughter), بِنْتُ الْأُخْتِ (sister's daughter); “my niece”: بِنْتُ أَخِي / بِنْتُ أُخْتِي.

absent.reason: No separate word: “my” is the suffix -ī (after a vowel -ya) on the noun.
absent.use: كِتَابِي (my book), أُمِّي (my mother), غُرْفَتِي (my room); the same suffix on عِنْدَ: عِنْدِي (I have).

absent.reason: No separate word: “your” is a suffix, -ka to a man and -ki to a woman.
absent.use: كِتَابُكَ (your book, to a man), كِتَابُكِ (to a woman); أَبُوكَ / أَبُوكِ (your father).

absent.reason: No separate word: “his” is the suffix -hu (-hi after i or y).
absent.use: كِتَابُهُ (his book), أَبُوهُ (his father), عِنْدَهُ (he has).

absent.reason: No separate word: “her” is the suffix -hā.
absent.use: كِتَابُهَا (her book), أُمُّهَا (her mother), عِنْدَهَا (she has).

absent.reason: No separate word: “our” is the suffix -nā.
absent.use: بَيْتُنَا (our house), أُسْرَتُنَا (our family), عِنْدَنَا (we have).

absent.reason: No separate word: “your” (several people) is the suffix -kum (-kunna for women only).
absent.use: بَيْتُكُمْ (your house), عِنْدَكُمْ (you have); to women only: بَيْتُكُنَّ.

absent.reason: No separate word: “their” is the suffix -hum (-hunna for women only; -him after i or y).
absent.use: بَيْتُهُمْ (their house), عِنْدَهُمْ (they have); women only: بَيْتُهُنَّ.
